title: Bias and Representational Harm in LLMs

questions.question: How does the lesson distinguish representational harm from allocational harm?
options: Representational harm only shows up in vision-language models that generate images, while allocational harm is limited to purely text-based LLMs
Representational harm is measured with embedding-based metrics only, while allocational harm is measured with probability-based metrics only
Representational harm is stereotypes, erasure, or demeaning portrayal (like depicting nurses as exclusively female); allocational harm is unequal material outcomes for a group
Allocational harm only occurs in offline batch scoring, such as resume screening, and never appears in a live conversational deployment
questions.explanation: The lesson defines representational harm as stereotypes, erasure, or demeaning portrayal (e.g. depicting nurses as exclusively female), while allocational harm is unequal material outcomes for a group (e.g. scoring one group's resumes systematically lower) -- these are distinct from the evaluation-metric categories and from deployment context.

questions.question: Which of these are the three evaluation-metric categories from Gallegos et al. 2024?
options: Embedding-based (WEAT-style association tests), probability-based (stereotype completion likelihoods), and generated-text-based (downstream-task measurement)
Pre-RLHF, mid-RLHF, and post-RLHF measurement stages, tracking how the same bias metric changes at each step of the alignment and fine-tuning pipeline
Vision-based, audio-based, and text-based metrics, split according to which input modality the model under evaluation accepts
WEAT, BLEU, and ROUGE scores, borrowed directly from the embedding-association and machine-translation evaluation literature
questions.explanation: Gallegos et al. 2024, as the lesson describes it, categorize bias-evaluation metrics into embedding-based (WEAT-style association tests), probability-based (stereotype-confirming vs violating completion likelihoods), and generated-text-based (downstream-task measurement on generated output) -- not by RLHF stage, modality, or borrowed MT metrics.

questions.question: Why is intersectional fairness evaluation needed in addition to single-axis evaluation?
options: Intersectionality is just another term for k-fold cross-validation applied to demographic subgroups instead of random splits
Bias that only emerges at intersections, like gender x race, is missed by evaluations that look at just one axis at a time
Single-axis measures are computationally cheaper to run, so intersectional evaluation is only a cost-saving shortcut, not a coverage fix
Single-axis evaluation is the only approach permitted under current data-protection regulations, so intersectional analysis is legally restricted
questions.explanation: The lesson's An et al. 2025 example shows Black women scoring best and Black men scoring worst on automated resume evaluation -- a pattern invisible to gender-only or race-only evaluation and detectable only by looking at the gender x race intersection, not a cost or legal question.

questions.question: What does WinoIdentity (COLM 2025) introduce?
options: An adversarial attack framework designed to fool automated demographic classifiers into misreading a speaker's protected attributes during moderation
A new subword tokenizer optimized to represent identity terms and named entities more efficiently than standard BPE vocabularies
A drop-in replacement for WEAT that runs the same embedding-association test directly against generated text instead of static embeddings
An uncertainty-based fairness measure for coreference resolution across intersectional identity tuples, not just point predictions
questions.explanation: The lesson describes WinoIdentity as extending Winogender/WinoBias-style coreference-resolution bias evaluation to intersectional identities with an uncertainty-based fairness measure, testing whether the model's confidence over pronoun-referent choices differs across intersectional identity tuples -- not an attack tool, tokenizer, or WEAT variant.

questions.question: Which of these is a mechanistic-interpretability approach to bias?
options: Switching the alignment algorithm from PPO-based RLHF to DPO, which changes preference optimization but doesn't inspect internal representations
Increasing the KL-divergence regularization coefficient during fine-tuning to keep the aligned model closer to its pretrained reference
Identifying gender-correlated neurons in FFN-value, FFN-query, and attention-value layers, or using sparse autoencoders to surface race-correlated features
Re-labeling the training dataset with more balanced demographic annotations and rerunning the same fine-tuning pipeline from scratch
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Yu & Ananiadou 2025 identifying gender-correlated neurons in FFN-value, FFN-query, and attention-value layers, and Ahsan & Wallace 2025 using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to surface race-correlated features -- both mechanistic interventions on the model's internals, unlike algorithm swaps, regularization tweaks, or relabeling.

questions.question: What does the 10-year meta-critique (arXiv:2508.11067) argue about the bias literature?
options: It disproportionately focuses on binary-gender bias, leaving axes like disability, religion, and migration status under-examined
It avoids quantitative methods entirely, relying only on qualitative case studies and reader testimonials to make its argument
It overemphasizes intersectionality at the expense of simpler, more actionable single-axis bias metrics that practitioners can readily apply
It is balanced across all identity axes, giving disability, religion, and migration status the same amount of attention as gender
questions.explanation: The lesson summarizes the meta-critique as finding that a decade of bias literature disproportionately focuses on binary-gender bias, while axes like disability, religion, migration status, and multi-lingual identity receive far less attention -- risking harm to those groups through neglect, not through excess quantification or excess intersectional focus.
